A hatch is a small opening or doorway — one that is built into a flat surface like a floor, a ceiling, a wall, or the deck of a ship — and that usually has a cover or door that you can open and close over it.

Think of it as a hidden or built-in gateway between two spaces, designed to let a person or things pass through when needed, but which stays closed the rest of the time.

1. An opening in a floor, ceiling, deck, or roof

This is the most common meaning. A hatch is an access point cut into a surface that you normally walk on, stand under, or sit on top of. It connects one level or compartment to another.

  • A ship has hatches on its deck — rectangular openings through which cargo is loaded into the hold below, or through which crew members can climb down.
  • A submarine has hatches on its top — the round doors you see sailors climbing through when a sub is on the surface.
  • Many homes have a loft hatch (also called an attic hatch) — a small opening in the ceiling that you push open to get into the attic space above.
  • Old houses often had a cellar hatch in the floor — a trapdoor-like opening that led down to the storage area below.

In all these cases, the hatch serves the same purpose: it is a built-in opening that allows access to a space that is otherwise closed off.

The word can refer to the opening itself, or to the lid/door that covers it — both uses are correct and common. So "open the hatch" means either opening the cover or passing through the opening. Context makes it clear.

2. A small window-like opening cut into a wall (a serving hatch)

A hatch doesn't always have to be in a floor or ceiling. It can also be a small rectangular opening cut through a wall — usually so that things can be passed through from one room to another without anyone having to walk around.

The most familiar example is a serving hatch: an opening cut through the wall between a kitchen and a dining room, so that a person in the kitchen can pass food directly through the wall to someone in the dining room. Many older homes and traditional restaurants have these.

The key idea here is the same — a hatch is an opening that allows passage (of people or things) without the need to use a full door.
Escape Hatch — a very important phrase

You will often hear the phrase escape hatch. This literally refers to a hatch on an aircraft, spacecraft, submarine, or tank that is specifically designed to be used in emergencies — a way to get out quickly when the normal exit is unavailable or blocked.

In everyday language, "escape hatch" is also used figuratively to mean a way out of a difficult situation — a backup plan, a loophole, or an option that lets you get out of a commitment or a problem. For example: "The vague wording of the contract gave the company an escape hatch."
The Hatch on a Ship — worth understanding fully

Ships deserve a bit more detail here because the word is most strongly associated with maritime use.

On a ship, a hatch (also called a hatchway) is a large opening on the deck (the flat top surface of the ship). It is covered by a hatch cover — a heavy lid or a series of panels that seal it shut. When cargo needs to be loaded or unloaded, the hatch cover is removed and goods are lowered into or lifted out of the cargo hold below.

The phrase "batten down the hatches" comes from seafaring — before a storm, sailors would seal the hatch covers tightly (using wooden strips called battens) so that water couldn't get in. Today, this phrase is used figuratively to mean "prepare for something difficult or dangerous that is coming."

• In aviation and spacecraft: rockets, capsules, and space stations have hatches — the round or oval doors that astronauts use to enter, exit, or move between modules. These are designed to seal airtight.
  • In military vehicles: tanks and armored vehicles have hatches on top through which the crew can poke their heads out or exit the vehicle.
  • In art: a hatch (and especially cross-hatch) refers to one of a series of fine, parallel lines drawn close together to create the effect of shadow or shading in a drawing or engraving. Multiple parallel lines are collectively called hatching, and overlapping lines in two directions are called cross-hatching.
  • A brood: less commonly, "hatch" can also refer to the group of young animals — typically birds or fish — that came from a set of eggs all at once. For example, "The whole hatch of chicks was healthy."

One Line to Remember It By

A hatch is a small built-in opening — in a floor, wall, ceiling, or deck — that connects one space to another and can be opened and closed, and by extension, anything resembling or functioning like such an opening.
